When the porters wife announced that a gentleman and a lady wished to see me, I had, the wish being father to the thought, an immediate vision of sitters who had come for portraits. <break time="0.8s" /> The visitors, a tall, straight gentleman of about fifty and a slim, handsome lady, were dressed with such care and quiet distinction that I took it for granted they had come to be painted. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet when the lady said that they had come from Mister Rivet, a landscape painter I knew, the gentleman hesitated for a long moment before he could bring himself to state their errand. <break time="0.8s" /> I was then an illustrator for magazines and popular novels, but I could not get out of my head the honours, to say nothing of the rewards, of a great painter of portraits. <break time="0.8s" /> Illustration was my pot boiler, the work that paid the rent, and so it was with a sinking heart that I began to suspect these splendid strangers were not customers at all. <break time="0.8s" /> At last the Major, for such he proved to be, explained with painful frankness that they had lost their money and that they hoped to earn something as models for an artist like me. <break time="0.8s" /> We thought that if you ever have to do people like us, we might be something like it, said the Major, adding that his wife would be particularly good as a lady in a book. <break time="0.8s" /> Looking at them, so tall and so correct, I saw at once what they meant, for they were exactly the kind of people that my illustrations were always trying, and often failing, to suggest.

They had spent twenty years visiting country houses, where the Major had shot in the finest woods and his wife had walked through wet gardens, dressed perfectly for every occasion, but all of that was gone. <break time="0.8s" /> Their small income was not enough to live on, and, having no talent for any trade, they seemed to believe that the only thing left to sell was the very look of their class. <break time="0.8s" /> They were, in short, the real thing, a gentleman and a lady, and I had to admit that in appearance, at least, nothing could have been more genuine than the pair before me. <break time="0.8s" /> Still, a question troubled me as I studied them, for I had found again and again that what a model really is matters far less than what she can be made to seem. <break time="0.8s" /> My regular model, Miss Churm, was only a freckled young woman from the London streets, yet she could represent anything, from a fine lady to a shepherdess, with an ease that seemed almost magical. <break time="0.8s" /> Meeting her in the studio, Missus Monarch could hardly hide her surprise that so ordinary a girl should play a lady, but when I asked her to become a Russian princess, Miss Churm was transformed in a moment. <break time="0.8s" /> It was precisely because she was not a lady that she could seem one, and I began to wonder whether a model who already possessed every quality might, by that very fact, have nothing left to give. <break time="0.8s" /> Nevertheless, having been offered the drawings for a splendid edition of Philip Vincents novels, I agreed to try the Monarchs, since its first book, Rutland Ramsay, was full of gentlemen and ladies.

Missus Monarch sat with a stillness that no professional could have equalled, yet, however I arranged her, she always came out the same, a tall, elegant figure who looked less like a character than like a photograph. <break time="0.8s" /> She was the real thing, but always the same thing, and I came to feel that her very perfection was a kind of prison from which no character in any story could escape. <break time="0.8s" /> The Major was no more useful, for, being six feet two and impossible to bend into any other shape, he could be employed only for the representation of brawny giants. <break time="0.8s" /> When I asked them to put on costumes, they would do so obediently, yet in a borrowed coat or a peasants shawl they somehow looked more like themselves than ever, the gentleman and lady stubbornly shining through. <break time="0.8s" /> Miss Churm, by contrast, could put on any role as easily as a hat, and the lady in my drawings, though Miss Churm was nothing of the kind, looked more like a lady than Missus Monarch ever did. <break time="0.8s" /> The truth, which I had always half known, now became painfully plain, namely that I had an innate preference for the represented subject over the real one, since the defect of the real one was so often a lack of representation. <break time="0.8s" /> Only then did I understand why my best ladies had always been drawn from a girl who was not a lady at all, for an artist needs not what is, but what can be imagined. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet I could not bring myself to send the Monarchs away, so patient were they, so eager to please, and so quietly anxious every morning when they climbed the stairs to my studio.

One day a young Italian who had been selling penny ices from a small green handcart appeared at my door, and though he spoke hardly a word of English, I took him on as both servant and model. <break time="0.8s" /> His name was Oronte, and before long this cheerful seller of ices, dressed in borrowed English clothes, was posing as the hero of Rutland Ramsay, and looking every inch a gentleman. <break time="0.8s" /> The Major, finding his place taken by a former street seller, asked me with forced lightness whether this was my idea of an English gentleman, and I could see how deeply the question hurt him. <break time="0.8s" /> To be placed below a servant and a cockney girl was a humiliation that no one of their class could have imagined, yet they bore it in silence, still hoping that their turn would come. <break time="0.8s" /> Then my friend Jack Hawley, a painter whose judgment I trusted, returned from abroad, and, looking over the Rutland Ramsay drawings with a fresh eye, he declared that the work was simply bad. <break time="0.8s" /> They will not do, he said of the Monarchs, warning me in his blunt way that I must get back into my boat at once or I would go straight to the bottom. <break time="0.8s" /> The warning was serious, for the publishers had also begun to doubt my drawings, and my share in the rest of the series was to depend entirely on the satisfaction I should give with the first book. <break time="0.8s" /> I knew that Hawley was right, and yet so much did I pity the Monarchs that, for a while longer, I kept them on, giving them the minor parts and telling myself that they might still improve.
